flashcards.q: State React Testing Library's core philosophy in one sentence.
flashcards.a: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you" -- query and interact like a real user, assert on user-visible outcomes, not implementation details.

flashcards.q: What is RTL's query priority ranking, from preferred to last resort?
flashcards.a: getByRole/getByLabelText/getByText (accessible, preferred) > getByPlaceholderText/getByAltText (acceptable fallback) > getByTestId (last resort -- friction here signals a real accessibility gap in the component).

flashcards.q: Why is userEvent generally preferred over fireEvent in RTL tests?
flashcards.a: userEvent simulates the full realistic event sequence a real interaction produces (pointer down, focus, pointer up, click), while fireEvent dispatches a single minimal synthetic event -- some bugs only manifest given the full sequence.

flashcards.q: Why does MSW intercept at the network layer instead of mocking fetch or an API client module?
flashcards.a: Network-layer interception (via a real Service Worker or Node interceptor) means the application code makes a genuinely real request that happens to be intercepted, so the same mock handlers work identically across unit, integration, E2E tests, and even local dev -- module mocking creates per-test-file fakes that can drift from reality.

flashcards.q: What does Playwright's auto-waiting eliminate, and what does it NOT eliminate?
flashcards.a: Eliminates the historically biggest E2E flake source: asserting against the DOM before an async update resolves (locators/assertions retry until the condition is met or timeout). Does NOT eliminate shared-test-state or genuine environment/timing variance flakiness.

flashcards.q: What is the testing trophy (Kent C. Dodds) and what specific problem is it a reaction to?
flashcards.a: Puts integration tests as the widest layer instead of unit tests, based on the observation that most real bugs live in the connections between units, not inside isolated functions. Reaction to pyramid-shaped suites with high unit coverage numbers that still missed whole bug classes.

flashcards.q: What are the two well-documented causes of visual regression test flakiness, and their fixes?
flashcards.a: 1) Font rendering/anti-aliasing/sub-pixel positioning differ by OS/GPU -- fix: generate and compare baselines exclusively in a consistent Docker environment, never locally. 2) Dynamic content (timestamps, random IDs) -- fix: explicit masking/exclusion regions before comparison.

flashcards.q: Name the three compounding causes of E2E suite rot.
flashcards.a: 1) Shared/mutable test state causing cross-test interference (worse as suite grows). 2) Timing/environment variance (slow CI runners, real third-party service latency). 3) Maintenance cost scaling faster than caught-bug value -- every UI change potentially breaks every E2E test touching that flow.

flashcards.q: Why can a test suite be 100% green while the feature is visibly broken in the browser?
flashcards.a: Tests assert on implementation details (internal state, DOM structure) that remain technically true even though user-facing behavior is broken. RTL's query-and-interact-like-a-user philosophy structurally prevents this since assertions can only target things actually visible/operable in rendered output.

flashcards.q: When is getByTestId the right choice in RTL?
flashcards.a: Only when no accessible query (role, label, text) can reliably identify the element and adding proper semantic markup isn't feasible for that case -- a genuine last resort, not a default first choice.

flashcards.q: What's the recommended remediation approach for a 40-minute, 15%-flaky E2E suite?
flashcards.a: Audit and move coverage that doesn't need a real browser+network+backend down to RTL+MSW integration tests, isolate test data per run (not shared fixtures), parallelize remaining E2E across CI workers, and quarantine/investigate genuinely flaky tests rather than letting them be routinely re-run and ignored.

flashcards.q: Why do large, full-component-tree Jest snapshots become low-value testing over time?
flashcards.a: They change on almost any legitimate change (a new class name, a wrapper div), so reviewers develop the habit of running --updateSnapshot and approving without reading the diff — the human verification step the snapshot depends on gets trained out by its own noisiness. Snapshots earn their keep on small, stable, low-churn output, not entire render trees.

flashcards.q: What does mutation testing measure that line coverage doesn't, and what's its practical cost tradeoff?
flashcards.a: Line coverage only confirms a line executed, not that a test asserted on its consequence correctly. Mutation testing (Stryker) introduces deliberate bugs and reports what % of mutants tests actually catch — a stronger signal, but computationally expensive, so typically run as a periodic/targeted audit rather than a per-PR blocking gate.
